learningObjective: Identify when CSE is legal given side effects and availability.

canonicalClaims.claim: CSE for memory loads requires proving that no intervening operation writes to the aliased memory; without this proof (via alias analysis or function purity attributes), the redundant load must be preserved.
conditions: IR distinguishes read/write memory operations and function memory effects.
Alias analysis or attribute annotations must support the no-alias/readonly proof.
nonImplications: Does not imply CSE always improves performance; increased register pressure can offset the win.
Does not imply loads are inherently side-effecting; volatile/atomic loads are, ordinary loads are not.

misconceptions.claim: SSA form guarantees that repeated loads from the same pointer are equivalent.
misconceptions.whyWrong: SSA operates on virtual registers; memory contents at a pointer can change independently of SSA renaming.

misconceptions.claim: Compilers assume functions are pure by default and treat calls as CSE-able.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The default assumption is that a call may read and write memory; purity requires explicit annotation (readnone/readonly) or interprocedural proof.

misconceptions.claim: Loads can never be CSE'd because they access memory.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Non-volatile, non-atomic loads can be CSE'd when availability is proven; only volatile/atomic loads carry ordering side effects.

implementationFacts: LLVM readnone: does not read or write memory; readonly: only reads; writeonly: only writes.
GVN (Global Value Numbering) is the modern generalization of CSE that reasons about equivalence classes.
performanceScenarios: Hot loops with repeated indexed reads benefit from CSE / GVN, provided intervening writes can be proven not to alias.
